source.title: Tracing Stereotypes from Representation to Output in Multilingual LLMs
source.authors: Ariun-Erdene Tumurchuluun; Yusser Al Ghussin; Pinzhen Chen; Josef van Genabith; Koel Dutta Chowdhury

record.tranche_reason: The study measures SAE-derived features in multilingual LLMs and reports that their lexical alignment and ablation effects vary substantially across SAE suites, refining claims that such features have stable, uniform interpretations. It does not test toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The study measures probe decodability and attribution influence, selects SAE features, analyzes their semantic and lexical properties, and ablates them. Its layer-wise probe and attribution findings do not measure superposition geometry, so they are not catalog rows for these versions. The SAE results are relevant to recoverable dictionary features and to the scope of claims about SAE features as stable units.
record.test_reason: The study uses off-the-shelf SAEs as a tool to find stereotype-related features and reports their gloss, lexical-anchor and bias-ablation properties. It does not test whether dictionaries recover a model's features (V4). It does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units (V5): there is no run-to-run, cross-width or feature-matching comparison. Features are hand-picked by contrastive selection (top-3 per cell), so gloss and anchor rates describe the selected subset. Cross-suite differences are confounded, as the authors stress. The measured quantities are bias-effect transfer and logit-lens alignment, not the superposition claim's constructs.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Decodability peaks 36–53% of depth before attribution. Selected Llama-Scope features are mostly category-linked, but ablation effects vary in sign and size across suites. 6–18% are language-agnostic, none category-agnostic. The language-agnostic advantage holds only in Llama-Scope.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses linear probes, attribution patching, pre-trained SAEs, and feature ablation in multilingual LLMs rather than testing the toy-network superposition setup. The SAEs are off-the-shelf models and were not trained by the authors.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary across SAE suites. The study reports suite-dependent lexical alignment and ablation effects; the cross-language advantage for language-agnostic features appears in Llama-Scope, is absent in Llama-Multi and Qwen-Multi, and reverses for English and Spanish in Gemma-Scope.

fits_no_version.finding: On the same base model, Llama-Scope and Llama-Multi SAEs give very different properties for contrastively selected features. Unembedding alignment is 46.9% vs 8.8%, and mean ablation Δbias is −0.055 vs +0.0002. The suites also differ in L0 (50 vs ≈10,827), data and language.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Properties and causal effects of concept-selected SAE features depend on the SAE suite chosen, even for one base model.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-feature ablations of selected SAE features give bidirectional, mostly small bias changes. No feature has category-agnostic effects, and only 6–18% have language-agnostic effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ablation effects of individual SAE features on a downstream behaviour are heterogeneous and rarely transfer across categories.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Only 8B–9B models and four high-resource languages are studied; SHADES intervention results cover three languages. SAE suites differ in multiple confounded properties, and the authors note that this complicates comparisons. Feature ablations are individual, so redundancy in bias pathways is not addressed. The study does not test completeness or run-to-run stability of SAE features.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant rows omitted. Probe and attribution-patching results concern where stereotype information is decodable or estimated to influence outputs, not the claim versions about superposition or SAE feature units.

untested.parts: No toy models, geometry or sparsity transition.
Assumes SAEs recover features. There is no measure of feature spread across neurons, and no reconstruction or interpretability rate over unselected features.
No completeness, run-to-run stability, cross-width or cross-suite feature matching. Suite differences are confounded (base model, width, L0, data).
No comparison of 1-D vs multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T5 to uses_without_test/T4. The reader's labels were dropped: the V4 'supports' rested on selection-dependent gloss and anchor rates. The V5 'limits_scope' rested on bias-transfer scores and cross-suite differences the authors call confounded, which are not V5's stability or canonicity constructs. Superposition is not discussed in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature overlap or near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent geometric transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
The study does not test neuron polysemanticity as a consequence of limited capacity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The study does not test causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.

The study finds interpretable SAE-selected features in real models, but does not measure how many neurons encode each feature or establish that the features exhaustively describe model representations.

It reports variation across SAE suites in lexical anchoring and intervention effects, but does not test feature completeness, run-to-run stability, or canonical correspondence between features from different dictionaries.
The study does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of retained Llama-Scope SAE features whose lexical-anchor cosine exceeded the suite's chance threshold.
rows.note: Feature-level lexical alignment was measured using cosine similarity to the unembedding rows.
rows.check: Lexical-anchor rate (46.9%) of contrastively selected Llama-Scope features. Logit-lens alignment of a selected subset does not measure whether an SAE recovers the model's features or whether features are canonical. 'Observed' has no referent in any version.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of retained Llama-Multi SAE features whose lexical-anchor cosine exceeded the suite's chance threshold.
rows.note: This differs markedly from Llama-Scope, although both suites use the same base model; the paper notes that the suites also differ in training and configuration.
rows.check: Same as R1 (8.8%, Llama-Multi). Low unembedding alignment is not evidence against feature recovery, since mid-layer features need not align with output tokens. 'Partial' is unfounded.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of retained Gemma-Scope SAE features whose lexical-anchor cosine exceeded the suite's chance threshold.
rows.note: The paper cautions that SAE suites differ in sparsity, training data, and dictionary configuration.
rows.check: Same as R1 (41.7%, Gemma-Scope); anchor rate of selected features only.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of retained Qwen-Multi SAE features whose lexical-anchor cosine exceeded the suite's chance threshold.
rows.note: The result is much lower than for Gemma-Scope; the suites differ in several properties.
rows.check: Same as R2 (0.8%, Qwen-Multi). The suite has L0≈26,893, so it is barely sparse; the measure does not bear on the versions.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared available Llama-Scope feature glosses with the social category used to select each feature.
rows.measure: Glossed features on-concept for their selected social category
rows.note: The paper also describes recurring semantic families within categories.
rows.check: 123/139 on-concept glosses is a selection-dependent value. Features were chosen for category contrast, and glosses exist only for a Neuronpedia-glossed subset. No baseline or control is given.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Individually zero-masked selected SAE features in the residual stream during inference and measured SHADES bias change.
rows.measure: Mean ablation effect on bias (∆bias); mean Cohen's d
rows.uncertainty: One-sample t-tests and bootstrap confidence intervals were used; row-specific values not stated.
rows.note: Effects were heterogeneous and bidirectional; the table reports 9.6% of feature–bias-type pairs with significant reductions.
rows.check: Mean Δbias from single-feature ablation measures bias effects of selected features, not superposition or feature canonicity. Table 4 Cohen's d is −0.0709.

rows.uncertainty: One-sample t-tests and bootstrap confidence intervals were used; row-specific values not stated.
rows.note: The mean effect is smaller than for Llama-Scope; individual effects can have either sign.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Classified per-feature intervention effects using the Language Specificity Score threshold.
rows.note: The paper says all evaluated features were category-dependent under its CSS criterion.
rows.check: LSS classifies cross-language consistency of a feature's bias-ablation effect. This is not stability of the feature across SAE runs, which is what V5 names.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean cross-language ablation effects for language-agnostic and language-dependent features.
rows.measure: Measured bias reduction by evaluation language
rows.value: Language-agnostic features reduced measured bias by 46–79%; language-dependent features by 32–55%.
rows.note: The paper reports that this advantage did not replicate across the other SAE suites.
rows.check: Compares bias reduction of language-agnostic vs language-dependent features (46–79% vs 32–55%). This is a bias-mitigation comparison, not a version's construct.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean cross-language ablation effects for language-agnostic and language-dependent features.
rows.measure: Whether language-agnostic features had larger mean ablation effects
rows.value: The larger-effect pattern did not replicate.
rows.note: The text says the Llama-Scope advantage was absent in Llama-Multi.
rows.check: As R18; the pattern is absent in Llama-Multi.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The tested SAE suites and selected stereotype-related feature sets
reader_labels.reason: The study reports category-related glosses and above-threshold lexical anchoring for selected SAE features, providing evidence that dictionaries recover interpretable sparse features in these models (R1, R3, R5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Lexical anchoring differs substantially between suites, including suites on the same Llama base model, so the evidence does not generalize uniformly across dictionaries (R1-R4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The tested SAE suites and SHADES ablation setting
reader_labels.reason: Lexical alignment, average ablation effects, and transfer patterns vary across suites; language-agnostic features have larger effects only in Llama-Scope, while the pattern is absent or reversed elsewhere (R1-R4, R6-R9, R10-R21).
